s: delusion causes samsâra (through birth and death)
q: Through delusion he is born, dies, &c.' Being conversant with the deliberation about this delusion, one is conversant with the samsâra; being not conversant with that deliberation, one is not conversant with the samsâra.

s: sexual intercourse is not sought by fool
q: He who is clever, should not seek after sexual intercourse.

s: men do not reach final liberation (on account of their sinfulness)
q: on account of their sinfulness they do not reach liberation.

s: living beings experience pleasant and unpleasant feelings (when dwelling in darkness)
q: There are said to be blind beings dwelling in darkness; once or frequently meeting this lot, they experience pleasant and unpleasant feelings.

s: world contains many pains (for creatures)
q: many pains (are the lot) of the creatures.

s: men come to destruction through body (when given to their lusts)
q: Men who are given to their lusts, come to destruction through their weak, frail body.

s: doctrine of renunciation is proclaimed renunciation (by the speaker)
q: I shall proclaim the doctrine of renunciation.

s: parents lament children leaving the world (when their children proceed on the glorious road)
q: The lamenting parents say to them who proceed on the glorious road: 'Do not leave us!'

s: parents cry children leaving the world (consulting their own pleasure and indulging their passions)
q: Consulting their own pleasure, indulging their passions, 'making a noise, the parents cry:' No man who leaves his parents is (fit to become) a flood-crossing sage!

s: monk is unable to persevere in a religious life
q: Though some know the misery of the world, have relinquished their former connections, have given up ease, live in chastity, and, whether monk or layman, thoroughly understand the law, they are not able (to persevere in a religious life).

s: monk bears hardships of a mendicant's life (patiently)
q: Accounting (for this treatment) by his former sins, knowing pleasant and unpleasant occurrences, he should patiently wander about.

s: layman understands doctrine and faith (thoroughly)
q: whether monk or layman, thoroughly understand the law

s: monk leads religious life (by giving up worldliness and bearing disagreeable feelings)
q: Quitting all worldliness one should bear all (disagreeable) feelings, being possessed of the right view.

s: doctrine and faith is a highest doctrine (declared for men)
q: This highest doctrine has here been declared for men.

s: monk collects alms (in all sorts of families)
q: Therefore a wise man should lead the life of an ascetic by collecting pure alms or any alms in all sorts of families.

s: self-control causes scarcity (of wants or karma)
q: The unclothed one, who effects scarcity (of his wants or of his karman), bears these and various other hardships.

s: great heroes bore hardships of a mendicant's life (in former years)
q: The great heroes (i.e. the Tîrthakaras) who for a long time walked in the former years, the worthy ones bore the troubles (mentioned above);

s: Tîrthakaras are great heroes
q: The great heroes (i.e. the Tîrthakaras)

s: doctrine and faith is safe refuge (for those in danger)
q: As an island which is never covered with water, so is the law taught by the noble ones (a safe refuge for those in danger).

s: teacher instructs disciples (regularly day and night)
q: The disciples are thus regularly instructed, day and night, by the knowledge-endowed great heroes, receiving knowledge from them.

s: disciples receive knowledge (from great heroes)
q: The disciples are thus regularly instructed, day and night, by the knowledge-endowed great heroes, receiving knowledge from them.

s: monk preaches doctrine and faith (to all sorts of creatures)
q: Not neglecting tranquillity, indifference, patience, liberation, purity, uprightness, gentleness, and freedom from worldly cares, one should, with due consideration, preach the law of the mendicants to all sorts of creatures.

s: monk does not injure living beings (including himself and the four kinds of living beings)
q: With due consideration preaching the law of the mendicants, one should do no injury to one's self, nor to anybody else, nor to any of the four kinds of living beings.

s: right faith causes victory (for the learned, wise, and steadfast hero)
q: Knowing them, the learned, the wise, the steadfast hero will always be victorious through the right faith.

s: death is desired as dissolution of the body (by the sage who has reached the other side)
q: The sage who has reached the other side, unafflicted and unmoved like a beam, being in the power of death, desires death as the dissolution of the body.

s: awakened one praises path to final liberation (for those who exert themselves, have forsworn cruelty, and are endowed with knowledge)
q: He praises the road to liberation for those who well exert themselves, who have forsworn cruelty, are zealous and endowed with knowledge.

s: great heroes are victorious victorious
q: Thus some great heroes are victorious;

s: men are attached to objects of the senses (when born in various families)
q: thus men, born in various families, cry bitterly because they are attached to the objects of the senses;

s: Seventh Lecture, Called Liberation contains lesson First Lesson
q: Seventh Lecture, Called Liberation. First Lesson.

s: Mahâvîra enjoins the three vows
q: 'By the Brahman, the wise (Mahâvîra), three vows have been enjoined.'

s: the three vows are enjoined by Mahâvîra
q: 'By the Brahman, the wise (Mahâvîra), three vows have been enjoined.'

s: houseless are called unfettered (when without desires and doing no harm)
q: A person who is without desires and does no harm unto any living beings in the whole world, is called by me 'unfettered.'

s: houseless should not desire forbidden things (those who are awakened)
q: Those who are awakened, should not wish for pleasure, nor do harm, nor desire (any forbidden things).

s: houseless do not harm living beings (in the whole world)
q: A person who is without desires and does no harm unto any living beings in the whole world, is called by me 'unfettered.'

s: houseless avoid sin (through disciplined conduct)
q: Practising thus the law as it has been declared, one becomes tranquil, averted from sin, guarded against the allurements of the senses.

s: houseless beg for clothes (permitted by the religious code)
q: He should beg for (clothes) which he wants, and which are permitted by the religious code;

s: houseless possess clothes (according to the prescribed outfit)
q: A mendicant who is fitted out with three robes, and a bowl as fourth (article), will not think: I shall beg for a fourth robe.

s: houseless possess alms-bowl (as an article of mendicant equipment)
q: A mendicant who is fitted out with three robes, and a bowl as fourth (article), will not think: I shall beg for a fourth robe.

s: houseless use straw (for a secluded resting place after examining and cleaning the ground)
q: After having repeatedly examined and cleaned the ground, where there are no eggs, nor living beings, nor seeds, nor sprouts, nor dew, nor water, nor ants, nor mildew, nor waterdrops, nor mud, nor cobwebs--he should spread the straw on it.

s: houseless reject fire (even when suffering from cold)
q: Yet it does not become me to kindle or light a fire, that I may warm or heat myself; nor (to procure that comfort) through the order of others.

s: houseless practice penance (aspiring to freedom from bonds)
q: A naked monk (should be) aspiring to freedom from bonds. Penance suits him.

s: houseless seek Nirvâna (through disciplined religious death)
q: Not devoted to any of the external objects he reaches the end of his life; thinking that patience is the highest good, he (should choose) one of (the described three) good methods of entering Nirvâna.

s: houseless endure religious death (without attachment to life or death)
q: should not long for life, nor wish for death he should yearn after neither, life or death

s: householders approach houseless (at designated austere places)
q: A householder may approach a mendicant who stays in any of these places, and say unto him: O long-lived Sramana!

s: householders injure living beings (when acting sinfully to provide offerings for mendicants)
q: This householder, forsooth, for my sake injures all sorts of living beings, to give me food, &c., clothes, &c., or to prepare pleasant lodgings.

s: householders provide food (sometimes obtained through injury to living beings)
q: I shall give you what I have bought or stolen or taken, though it was not to be taken, nor given, but was taken by force, viz. food, drink, dainties and spices, clothes, an alms-bowl, a plaid, a broom--by acting sinfully against all sorts of living beings;

s: living beings receive no pain pain (from a wise man)
q: Knowing (and renouncing) severally and singly the actions against living beings, in the regions above, below, and on the surface, everywhere and in all ways--a wise man neither gives pain to these bodies, nor orders others to do so, nor assents to their doing so.

s: doctrine and faith is declared by Mahâvîra (as the law known and seen with quick discernment)
q: Thus they are not well taught, not well instructed in the religion such as it has been declared by the Revered One, who knows and sees with quick discernment.

s: doctrine and faith opposes sin (by requiring its avoidance)
q: Everywhere sins are admitted; but to avoid them is called my distinction.

s: sin is avoided by doctrine and faith (as a defining distinction)
q: Everywhere sins are admitted; but to avoid them is called my distinction.

s: karman is destroyed by contemplation
q: He who is indifferent and wishes for the destruction of karman, should continue his contemplation.

s: desire is not wished for by those who are awakened
q: Those who are awakened, should not wish for pleasure, nor do harm, nor desire (any forbidden things).

s: Nirvâna is entered by houseless (through one of three good methods of religious death)
q: Not devoted to any of the external objects he reaches the end of his life; thinking that patience is the highest good, he (should choose) one of (the described three) good methods of entering Nirvâna.

s: penance suits houseless (when aspiring to freedom from bonds)
q: A naked monk (should be) aspiring to freedom from bonds. Penance suits him.

s: the body is dissolved by houseless (through exertion and reduction of food)
q: regularly reducing his food, and diminishing his sins, 'he should take proper care of his body, being immovable like a beam; exerting himself he dissolves his body.'

s: Mahâvîra is a wise Brahman (revered and enlightened)
q: 'By the Brahman, the wise (Mahâvîra), three vows have been enjoined.'

s: The Pillow of Righteousness is a lecture (called the Pillow of Righteousness)
q: Eighth Lecture, (Called) the Pillow of Righteousness.

s: Mahâvîra avoids sin (thoroughly knowing karman)
q: The Venerable One understands thus: he who is under the conditions (of existence), that fool suffers pain. Thoroughly knowing (karman), the Venerable One avoids sin.

s: Mahâvîra practices nonviolence (abstaining from killing)
q: Practising the sinless abstinence from killing, he did no acts, neither himself nor with the assistance of others; he to whom women were known as the causes of all sinful acts, he saw (the true state of the world).

s: Mahâvîra uses food (clean food)
q: Having got clean food, he used it, restraining the impulses.

s: Mahâvîra eats rice (rough food)
q: In summer he exposes himself to the heat, he sits squatting in the sun; he lives on rough (food): rice, pounded jujube, and beans.

s: Mahâvîra eats jujube (pounded and part of rough food)
q: In summer he exposes himself to the heat, he sits squatting in the sun; he lives on rough (food): rice, pounded jujube, and beans.

s: Mahâvîra eats beans (rough food)
q: In summer he exposes himself to the heat, he sits squatting in the sun; he lives on rough (food): rice, pounded jujube, and beans.

s: Mahâvîra endures pain (free from desire and undisturbed)
q: Bearing all hardships, the Venerable One, undisturbed, proceeded (on the road to Nirvâna).

s: Mahâvîra proceeds toward Nirvâna (bearing all hardships)
q: Bearing all hardships, the Venerable One, undisturbed, proceeded (on the road to Nirvâna).

s: Mahâvîra lodges in resting-places (for thirteen long years)
q: In these places was the wise Sramana for thirteen long years; he meditated day and night, exerting himself, undisturbed, strenuously.

s: resting-places include workshops
q: He sometimes lodged in workshops, assembling-places, wells, or shops; sometimes in manufactories or under a shed of straw.

s: resting-places include burying-ground
q: He sometimes lodged in travellers' halls, garden-houses, or towns; sometimes on a burying-ground, in relinquished houses, or at the foot of a tree.

s: Mahâvîra is attacked by dogs (in Lâdha)
q: Even in the faithful part of the rough country the dogs bit him, ran at him.

s: inhabitants of Lâdha incite dogs (against monks)
q: Few people kept off the attacking, biting dogs. Striking the monk, they cried 'Khukkhû,' and made the dogs bite him.

s: dogs attack houseless (biting and tearing them)
q: Even thus armed they were bitten by the dogs, torn by the dogs.

s: Lâdha is difficult to travel in difficult to travel
q: It is difficult to travel in Lâdha.

s: houseless practice nonviolence (ceasing to use the stick against living beings)
q: Ceasing to use the stick (i.e. cruelty) against living beings, abandoning the care of the body, the houseless (Mahâvîra), the Venerable One, endures the thorns of the villages (i.e. the abusive language of the peasants), (being) perfectly enlightened.

s: heretical monks use robe (to bear the cold)
q: (Some heretical monks say), 'We shall put on more clothes; kindling wood or (well) covered, we shall be able (to bear) the very painful influence of the cold.'

s: Mahâvîra endures cold (despising all shelter)
q: But the Venerable One desired nothing of the kind; strong in control, he suffered, despising all shelter.

s: Mahâvîra endures heat (sitting squatting in the sun)
q: In summer he exposes himself to the heat, he sits squatting in the sun; he lives on rough (food): rice, pounded jujube, and beans.

s: Mahâvîra is a ascetic (Venerable Ascetic)
q: As I have heard it, I shall tell how the Venerable Ascetic, exerting himself and meditating, after having entered the order in that winter, wandered about,

s: Mahâvîra knows women (as the causes of all sinful acts)
q: Practising the sinless abstinence from killing, he did no acts, neither himself nor with the assistance of others; he to whom women were known as the causes of all sinful acts, he saw (the true state of the world).

s: Mahâvîra understands living beings (as imbued with life when narrowly inspected)
q: He comprehended that they are, if narrowly inspected, imbued with life, and avoided to injure them; he, the great Hero.

s: living beings are subject to karman (becoming individually sinners by their actions)
q: The immovable (beings) are changed to movable ones, and the movable beings to immovable ones; beings which are born in all states become individually sinners by their actions.

s: pain is endured by Mahâvîra (without resentment)
q: Always well controlled, he bore the different sorts of feelings; overcoming carelessness and pleasure, the Brâhmana wandered about, speaking but little.

s: Mahâvîra is a sage (free from attachment)
q: This is the rule which has often been followed by the wise Brâhmana, the Venerable One, who is free from attachment: thus proceed (the monks).

s: Mahâvîra practices meditation (strenuously)
q: In these places was the wise Sramana for thirteen long years; he meditated day and night, exerting himself, undisturbed, strenuously.

s: Mahâvîra leads religious life (without using cold water)
q: For more than a couple of years he led a religious life without using cold water; he realised singleness, guarded his body, had got intuition, and was calm.

s: Mahâvîra practices renunciation (as a naked, world-relinquishing, houseless sage)
q: For a year and a month he did not leave off his robe. Since that time the Venerable One, giving up his robe, was a naked, world-relinquishing, houseless (sage).

s: Mahâvîra gives up robe (after one year and one month)
q: For a year and a month he did not leave off his robe. Since that time the Venerable One, giving up his robe, was a naked, world-relinquishing, houseless (sage).

s: Mahâvîra avoids sin (thoroughly knowing (karman))
q: The Venerable One understands thus: he who is under the conditions (of existence), that fool suffers pain. Thoroughly knowing (karman), the Venerable One avoids sin.

s: monk avoids forbidden food (in contrast to one who does not)
q: A monk or a nun desiring to enter the abode of a householder for collecting alms, should not enter or leave it together with a heretic or a householder; or a monk who avoids all forbidden food, &c., together with one who does not. (7)

s: householder has abode of a householder (an abode)

s: food is impure impure and unacceptable (when affected by or mixed with living beings, mildew, seeds or sprouts, water, or dust)
q: they should not, even if they can get it, accept of such food, thinking that it is impure and unacceptable. (1)

q: A monk or a nun on a begging-tour should not accept as alms whatever herbs they recognise

q: recognises food, drink, dainties, and spices as affected by, or mixed up with, living beings

s: food contains mildew (when affected by or mixed up with it)
q: recognises food, drink, dainties, and spices as affected by, or mixed up with, living beings, mildew, seeds or sprouts

s: food contains seeds or sprouts (when affected by or mixed up with them)
q: recognises food, drink, dainties, and spices as affected by, or mixed up with, living beings, mildew, seeds or sprouts

s: food is wet with water (when offered in an impure condition)

s: Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra) translated by Hermann Jacobi
q: Akaranga Sutra (Âkârâṅga Sûtra), Book II, translated by Hermann Jacobi

s: householder gives food (out of respect for a Nirgrantha and in behalf of a fellow-ascetic)
q: A monk or a nun on a begging-tour should not accept food, &c., from a householder whom they know to give out of respect for a Nirgrantha, in behalf of a fellow-ascetic

s: Nirgrantha is respected by householder (when the householder gives out)
q: from a householder whom they know to give out of respect for a Nirgrantha

s: householder prepares food (for many Sramanas and Brâhmanas, guests, paupers, and beggars after counting them)
q: A monk or a nun should not accept of food, &c., which they know has been prepared by the householder for the sake of many Sramanas and Brâhmanas, guests, paupers, and beggars, after he has counted them

s: Sramanas are recipients of food (food prepared by a householder for many persons)

s: Brâhmanas are recipients of food (food prepared by a householder for many persons)

s: monk should not enter always liberal, always open houses (for the sake of food or drink)
q: A monk or a nun wishing to enter the abode of a householder with the intention of collecting alms, should not, for the sake of food or drink, enter or leave such always liberal, always open houses

s: nun should not enter always liberal, always open houses (for the sake of food or drink)

s: whole duty requires always exerting oneself (instructed in all its meanings and endowed with bliss)
q: This certainly is the whole duty of a monk or a nun in which one should, instructed in all its meanings and endowed with bliss, always exert oneself.

s: First Lecture, Called Begging of Food is a lecture
q: First Lecture, Called Begging of Food.

s: First Lecture, Called Begging of Food has part whole duty
q: This certainly is the whole duty of a monk or a nun in which one should, instructed in all its meanings and endowed with bliss, always exert oneself. Thus I say. (14)

s: female mendicant is a mendicant (female)
q: WHEN a male or a female mendicant, having entered the abode of a householder with the intention of collecting alms, recognises food, drink, dainties, and spices as affected by, or mixed up with, living beings, mildew, seeds or sprouts, or wet with water, or covered with dust--either in the hand or the pot of another--they should not, even if they can get it, accept of such food, thinking that it is impure and unacceptable. (1)

s: monk is on begging-tour
q: A monk or a nun on a begging-tour should not accept as alms whatever herbs they recognise, on examining them, as still whole, containing their source of life, not split longwise or broadwise, and still alive, fresh beans, living and not broken; for such food is impure and unacceptable. (3)

s: nun is a mendicant (female)
q: A monk or a nun on a begging-tour should not accept as alms whatever herbs they recognise, on examining them, as still whole, containing their source of life, not split longwise or broadwise, and still alive, fresh beans, living and not broken; for such food is impure and unacceptable. (3)

s: faithful householders possess alms-bowl (various kinds)
q: there are several faithful householders, &c., (all down to) servants: they have put (food) in some of their various vessels, as a pan, a pot, a winnowing basket, a basket, a precious vessel.

s: monk say unto (others) (who follow the same rules of conduct, or live in the same place, or wander from village to village)
q: Some mendicants say unto (others) who follow the same rules of conduct, or live in the same place, or wander from village to village

q: food of which only a part may be used, and which is not wanted by bipeds, quadrupeds, Sramanas, Brâhmanas, guests, paupers, and beggars

q: food of which only a part may be used, and which is not wanted by bipeds, quadrupeds, Sramanas, Brâhmanas, guests, paupers, and beggars

s: First Lecture, Called Begging of Food is a lecture (called Begging of Food)

s: monk beg drink (under seven rules)

s: monk should not use a lodging-place used by the householder (in which there are women, children, cattle, food, and drink)
q: A monk or a nun on a begging-tour should not use, for religious postures, a lodging-place used by the householder, in which there are women, children, cattle, food, and drink.

s: monk inspects lodging fitness (before using or spreading a bed or couch)
q: They should then well inspect and sweep (the floor), and circumspectly spread a perfectly pure bed or couch.

s: monk should not use any above-ground lodging-place (for religious postures)
q: Hence it has been said to the mendicant, &c., that he should use no above-ground lodging-place for religious postures, &c.

s: householder gives lodging-place (to mendicants and others)
q: They (accordingly) give lodging-places for the sake of many Sramanas and Brâhmanas, guests, paupers, and beggars, in workshops, chapels, temples, assembly halls, wells, houses or halls for shopkeeping or for keeping or building carriages, distilleries, houses where Darbha-grass, bark, trees, wood or charcoal are being worked, houses on burial-places, rooms for retirement near the place of sacrifice, empty houses, hill-houses, caves, stone-houses, or palaces.

s: householder prepares lodging-place (for the sake of a mendicant)
q: A monk or a nun, knowing that the layman has, for the sake of the mendicant, matted the lodging, whitewashed it, strewn it (with grass, &c.), smeared it (with cowdung), levelled, smoothed, or perfumed it (or the floor of it), should not use that lodging, which has been prepared by the giver himself, &c., for religious postures.

s: householder's abode contains women, children, cattle, food, and drink
q: A monk or a nun on a begging-tour should not use, for religious postures, a lodging-place used by the householder, in which there are women, children, cattle, food, and drink.

q: But if the lodging contains only few eggs or few living beings, &c., they may, after having inspected and cleaned it, circumspectly use it for religious postures, &c.

s: lodging-place is unfit for religious postures (when prepared or appropriated by the giver for the mendicant)
q: A monk or a nun, knowing that the layman has, for the sake of the mendicant, matted the lodging, whitewashed it, strewn it (with grass, &c.), smeared it (with cowdung), levelled, smoothed, or perfumed it (or the floor of it), should not use that lodging, which has been prepared by the giver himself, &c., for religious postures.

s: couches is acceptable monk (when free from eggs and living beings, light, movable, and well tied)

s: couches is unacceptable monk (when heavy, immovable, or not well tied)
q: 2. If the couch is free from eggs, living beings, but is heavy, they should not accept such a couch. (14) 3. s: lodging fitness requires inspection (of the lodging and its floor)

s: religious postures is used in lodging-place (by monks or nuns when the lodging is fit)

s: Sramanas receive lodging-place (along with guests, paupers, and beggars)
q: They (accordingly) give lodging-places for the sake of many Sramanas and Brâhmanas, guests, paupers, and beggars, in workshops, chapels, temples, assembly halls, wells, houses or halls for shopkeeping or for keeping or building carriages, distilleries, houses where Darbha-grass, bark, trees, wood or charcoal are being worked, houses on burial-places, rooms for retirement near the place of sacrifice, empty houses, hill-houses, caves, stone-houses, or palaces.

s: Kevalin explains lodging fitness (by giving reasons for restrictions)
q: The Kevalin says: This is the reason: Making secretions he might stumble or fall; stumbling or falling he might hurt his hand, &c. (II, I, 7, § 1), or any other limb of his body, or kill, &c., all sorts of living beings.

s: fire-body is affected by householder (when kindled, lighted, or extinguished for the householder's sake)
q: While the mendicant lives together with householders, the householder might, for his own sake, kindle or light or extinguish a fire-body.

s: living beings make lodging-place (unfit when present in great number)
q: A monk or a nun should not use, for religious postures, &c., sheds of grass or straw which contain eggs, living beings, &c. But they may do so if they contain few eggs, few living beings, &c.

s: varġakriyâ sin infects lodging-place (when ceded by other people after householders prepare lodgings for their own use)
q: if the reverend persons frequent such-like lodgings, viz. workshops, &c., and live in them which are ceded by other people (they should be warned): 'O long-lived one! that (lodging is infected by the sin called) vargakriyâ.'

s: monk does not use householder's abode (for religious postures, night's-rest, or study)

s: sâvadyakriyâ sin infects lodging-place (when lodgings are given for many sorts of Sramanas)

s: alpasâvadyakriyâ sin infects lodging-place (when householders prepare it for their own sake under the same circumstances)
q: 'O long-lived one! that (lodging is infected by the very small sin called) alpasâvadyakriyâ.'

s: monk does not accept food (in a house whose inhabitant's name and gotra are known)
q: A monk or a nun may know the name and gotra of him in whose lodging he lives; in that case they should not accept food, &c., in that house whether invited or not invited; for it is impure and unacceptable.

s: speech exists in real speech (while uttered)
q: that while uttered, it is (real) speech;

s: speech exists in subsequent non-existence (the moment after utterance)
q: that the moment after it has been uttered, the spoken speech is speech in (subsequent) non-existence.

s: monk should use true and accurate speech (when it is not sinful or blamable)
q: A monk or a nun, considering well, should use true and accurate speech, or speech which is neither truth nor untruth (i.e. injunctions); for such speech is not sinful, blamable, rough, stinging, &c.

s: nun should use speech that is neither truth nor untruth (when it is not sinful or blamable)
q: A monk or a nun, considering well, should use true and accurate speech, or speech which is neither truth nor untruth (i.e. injunctions); for such speech is not sinful, blamable, rough, stinging, &c.

s: monk should not use sinful speech (when rough, stinging, coarse, hard, or leading to harm)
q: A monk or a nun, well considering, should not use speech whether truth or untruth, or truth mixed with untruth, if it be sinful, blamable, rough, stinging, coarse, hard, leading to sins, to discord and factions, to grief and outrage, to destruction of living beings.

s: nun should not use sinful speech (when rough, stinging, coarse, hard, or leading to harm)

s: monk employs language moderation and restraint (with precision and after considering well)
q: Well considering (what one is to say), speaking with precision, one should employ language in moderation and restraint: the singular, dual, plural; feminine, masculine, neuter gender; praise, blame, praise mixed with blame, blame mixed with praise; past, present, or future (tenses), the first and second, or third (person).

s: nun employs language moderation and restraint (with precision and after considering well)
q: A monk or a nun, putting aside wrath, pride, deceit, and greed, considering well, speaking with precision, what one has heard, not too quick, with discrimination, should employ language in moderation and restraint.

s: man is addressed as monk (in sinless speech)

s: woman is addressed as lay-sister (in sinless speech)
